sentences.text: Rupa Bandopadhyay with Mr. Sujoy Sarkar, learned counsel, appears on his behalf and are ready to take up the hearing of the criminal appeal on merit.
Mr. Iqbal Kabir, learned counsel for the State who is appellant before this Court is heard on its merit.
Report of the learned Magistrate as well as the report of the learned Registrar (Administration) and so also the report of the Inspector-in-Charge, Bolpur P.S., District : Birbhum be kept on record.

The State of West Bengal/the appellant preferred this appeal against the judgment and order of conviction dated 12.3.1999 passed by the then SDJM, Bolpur, Birbhum, in connection with Case No.
C/60 of 1993 whereby and whereunder the respondent was convicted for the offence under Section 16(1)(A)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for having violated the provision of Section 7(i) of the P.F.A. Act because he was found selling and storing adulterated turmeric powder.
Charges under the said provision were framed on 29th March, 1997 to which the respondent had pleaded not guilty and claimed to be tried.

The prosecution examined Jahnabi Jiban Laha, Food Inspector, Bolpur Municipality, P.W.1. Dr. T.K. Kar, Assistant C.M.O.H. of Bolpur Local Health Authority and after close of the evidence the accused respondent herein was examined under section 313 Cr.P.C. in respect of incriminating evidence against him that on 17.8.1993 at around 9-00 a.m.
in his grocery shop he was found selling turmeric powder.

The defence of the respondent accused was one of denial of charge levelled against him, which emerged from the cross-examination of the prosecution witnesses and so also from his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
Learned Judge in his impugned judgment held the accused respondent herein guilty of the offence under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Indian Food Adulteration Act for violation of Section 7(1) of the P.F.A. Act and convicted under section 248(2) Cr.P.C. with direction to confiscate the seized alamats.

In so far as the impugned judgment and order of conviction relates, there is no denial as such and since no appeal ever filed on behalf of the respondent accused to challenge the order and judgment of conviction, I do not find any illegality in recording finding of facts and finding of guilt of the accused having committed the offence under the provision of the said Act.

Mr. Iqbal Kabir, learned counsel for the State/appellant has invited my attention to the order of sentence pointing out that the State has preferred this appeal simply on the ground of legality as to why the respondent accused was dealt with so leniently with the imposition of fine of Rs. 900/- only with the default clause for simple imprisonment whereas the provision prescribes that the fine should not be less than Rs. 2000/-.
This fact and the legal point are well taken into consideration by the learned Magistrate after having heard the accused respondent herein on the point of sentence.

The penalty as provided in Section 16 (1)(A)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act is imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year and which may extend to six years with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 2000/-.

Having carefully considered the statement of the convict and on hearing him on the question of sentence with the observation that he is a poor man and is living hand to mouth with the meagre income from his grocery shop and further having considered the condition of the convict and the The State Of West Bengal vs Narendra Nath Kundu on 10 July, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/101197999/
2 nature of the offence provided under the said Act, the learned Magistrate dealt with the sentence part by inflicting sentence with mercy.

sentences.text: It appears that sympathetic consideration was rooted in the judicial mind of the learned Magistrate.

The learned Magistrate considered the mitigating circumstance and considering that, sending the accused respondent herein behind the bar will not serve the purpose of justice and applying the principle of criminology and sociology and so also the principle of penology he dropped the idea of sending him to jail for a single day term and imposed fine of Rs. 900/- in default to S.I. for 40 days and sentenced to till rising of the Court (T.R.C.).
I am of the view that awarding sentence is the discretion of the learned Trying Magistrate.
I do find that enormity offence has to be taken into consideration, which was missing according to the learned Judge.
He has imposed sentence for his confinement till rising of the Court.
I do not find any illegality on that aspect.
However, so far as the imposition of fine is concerned, it ought to have been imposed with the fine of Rs. 2000/-.
Ergo, I modify the order of sentence to the extent that the respondent/convict accused shall pay fine of Rs. 2000/- in default to simple imprisonment for 40 days.
In the context above, this Govt. Appeal No. 6 of 2000 is allowed in part.
